title: Short Stuff: Peace Sign
summary: Short Stuff episode on the peace sign. Gerald Holtom, a British artist and conscientious objector, designed the symbol in 1958 for the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) march from Trafalgar Square to Aldermaston. Hosts explain it combines the semaphore letters N and D (nuclear disarmament). Holtom later said it depicted a despairing figure in the manner of Goya's peasant before a firing squad, which the hosts find doubtful. Holtom did not copyright the design, so it spread widely and was adopted by the hippie and Vietnam-era antiwar movements, then by women's rights, environmental, and anti-apartheid movements, and South Africa's government tried to ban it. Holtom wanted an inverted peace symbol on his headstone and did not get it. The episode closes with a tangent on the Mercedes-Benz logo, which the Daimler brothers adopted from a postcard their father sent them.

segments.title: Introduction
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode on the peace sign and briefly joke about who wrote the segment.

segments.title: Gerald Holtom and postwar nuclear fears
segments.summary: Holtom, a British artist and conscientious objector, created the symbol amid 1950s fears of nuclear war after the atomic bombings of Japan. Pacifist groups formed, including the Direct Action Committee against Nuclear War, which co-founded the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament.
topics: Direct Action Committee against Nuclear War

segments.title: The Aldermaston march and the logo
segments.summary: The CND organized a march from Trafalgar Square to Aldermaston, a nuclear material facility, and Holtom designed a logo for it.

segments.title: Semaphore origins and the Goya explanation
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the symbol combines the semaphore flag signals for N and D, standing for nuclear disarmament. Holtom's later claim that it depicted a figure in the manner of Goya's peasant before a firing squad does not match the painting, where the figure's arms are raised.

segments.title: Clay badges and lack of copyright
segments.summary: Holtom and the CND made badges from white baked clay meant to survive a nuclear war. Holtom did not copyright the design on purpose so it could spread widely.

segments.title: Spread through the hippie, antiwar, and civil rights movements
segments.summary: Without copyright, the symbol was adopted by hippies and expanded from nuclear disarmament to general peace, and by Vietnam-era protesters. It was later used by women's rights, environmental, and anti-apartheid movements, and South Africa's ruling government tried to ban it. Holtom wanted an inverted version on his headstone but did not get it.

segments.title: Holtom's headstone wish
segments.summary: The hosts and Chuck discuss Holtom's wish for an inverted peace symbol, which symbolized growth and the tree of life, and that his funeral planners did not honor it.

segments.title: Mercedes-Benz logo tangent
segments.summary: The hosts note the Mercedes-Benz logo predates the 1950s peace sign. The Daimler brothers adapted it from a postcard their father sent them, and the three points stand for land, sea, and air.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts end the short episode and credit iHeartRadio.
